title: Masses of Mistakes: Improving Y11 Revision
author: Quinn, Dani
summary: Dani Quinn examines why the common practice of sending Year 11 students home with large stacks of printed revision material tends to fail, walking through the likely outcomes: students carry it home and never open it, feel overwhelmed and never start, get frustrated and give up partway through, or complete it without any way of knowing whether their answers are right, potentially reinforcing errors. She argues teachers need to plan revision homework with the same rigor as any other task, weighing how long it will actually take including feedback, whether there's a built-in way for students to check their own accuracy, and whether the content targets students' strengths, which builds confidence and buy-in, or their weaknesses, which is better handled in class with support. Her practical suggestions include using platforms with automatic feedback like Sparx, providing annotated worked solutions rather than bare mark schemes, pre-empting what students should do when they get stuck, and setting smaller, more frequent chunks of work with clear check-in points. She closes with advice on communicating with parents, including reserving time early in the term for brief, low-stakes phone calls home before problems compound, and cautions that a hastily assembled past paper attempted too early in the course does more harm to confidence than good.
points: Quinn's core diagnosis is that big, unstructured revision packs fail not from laziness but from design flaws: no feedback loop, no differentiation by strength or weakness, and no visibility for the teacher into who has or hasn't engaged.
Her recommendation to target strengths for home revision and weaknesses for in-class, supported revision inverts the common assumption that homework should target gaps.
She frames early, brief parent phone calls, made "before disasters," as more time-efficient and more constructive than later, harder conversations once a student has fallen behind.
Her closing warning against "hastily cobbled together" past papers attempted mid-course names a specific harm: it normalizes not attempting questions and can erode confidence rather than build it.
quotes: Some strength training as they carry it home before dumping it somewhere in their room, never to be seen again. They feel as if they achieved something because they possess some ‘revision’ and the teacher feels like things are ok because they gave the pupils lots of work to do.
They complete lots of it, with no idea if it is correct or incorrect. They may well be practising getting it wrong, reinforcing mistakes and misconceptions.

If a pupil really struggles with trigonometry, written work on trig, completed at home with no support, is unlikely to improve their performance. It will probably just make them feel bad, if they can bear to start the work at all.

Annotated working is more valuable than simple mark schemes. You can print it or, to reduce printing, make it available online. This gives them better guidance on what ‘good’ looks like, and a meaningful example to look at if they are stuck.

Past papers or mixed revision hastily cobbled together is unlikely to be valuable. Attempting a past paper when only part-way through the course is demoralising and it teaches pupils it is normal not to try some questions.
